title: The juror whose vote decides
hook: Your clue says innocent. Is voting innocent the rational thing to do?

knows: a unanimous jury needs every vote to convict
doesNotKnow: that your vote matters only when you are pivotal, and being pivotal is itself evidence

misconception: A juror should simply vote what their own clue says.
objective: The learner can explain that under unanimity a juror's vote changes the verdict only when both others vote guilty, so in that case two guilty clues outweigh their one innocent clue and guilt is 70% likely, not the 30% their clue alone suggests.

claims.text: Under unanimity, your vote changes the verdict only when both other jurors vote guilty; otherwise one innocent vote already acquits.
claims.source: Rule: convict only if all three vote guilty. If either other juror votes innocent the verdict is acquit whatever you vote. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Rule check over all 8 vote patterns: verdict depends on your vote only when both others vote guilty.

claims.text: With clues right 70% of the time and an even prior (stated in the question), one innocent clue alone gives a 30% chance of guilt (stage: 'Your clue alone: 30%'); two guilty clues and one innocent give 70%, the same as one guilty clue alone.
claims.source: Bayes, builder's node check 2026-10-14: P(G | g guilty, i innocent) = 0.7^g 0.3^i / (0.7^g 0.3^i + 0.3^g 0.7^i). (g,i) = (0,1): 0.3; (2,1): 0.147/0.21 = 0.7; (1,0): 0.7. Matches the brief's check line. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Own node: P(G|g,i) with r = 0.7, prior 1/2: (0,1) = 0.30, (2,1) = 0.70, (1,0) = 0.70. | REWORDED v3 (builder, 2026-10-14): Numbers unchanged; the 30% is now a stage line and the prior is stated in the stem. Demo computes both with guilt(0,1) and guilt(2,1). Unverified. | FC pass 24 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Own Bayes by direct likelihood product (prior 1/2, r = 0.7): one innocent clue 0.300; guilty, guilty, innocent 0.700; one guilty 0.700 (also G,I,I 0.300 and I,I,I 0.073, the locked 7%). Stem now states the even prior; stage line 'Your clue alone: 30%' renders after the commit from guilt(0, 1); reveal prints guilt(2, 1) = 70% and guilt(0, 1) = 30%.

claims.text: On the stage the bar shows 7% guilt when both others vote innocent, 30% when they split and 70% when both vote guilty.
claims.source: Same formula: (0,3) = 0.027/0.37 = 0.073; (1,2) = 0.3. Assumes the other two vote their own clues (stage note 'votes own clue'), so their votes reveal their clues. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): DISPUTED: the stage does not show this. Demo.tsx sets pGuilt = guilt(g, 1), counting only your innocent clue and ignoring the others' innocent clues, so the bar labelled 'Chance of guilt from all three clues' reads 30% when both others vote innocent and 50% when they split (own node run of the Demo function). The correct values with sincere voting are guilt(g, 3 - g): 7% and 30%, as the claim and the Demo header comment say. Only the pivotal case (70%) is right. Fix (builder): pGuilt = guilt(g, 3 - g). | CLAIM FIX 2026-10-14 (demo-builder, W-194): Stage bug fixed: pGuilt = guilt(g, 3 - g) (was guilt(g, 1)), so the bar counts all three clues: (0,3) 7%, (1,2) 30%, (2,1) 70%. Claim text extended to include the 70% case the bar also shows. Needs an independent check. | FC pass 23 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Demo.tsx now sets pGuilt = guilt(g, 3 - g), with g = the others' guilty votes, and innocent clues = your 1 + (2 - g) = 3 - g, which is correct under the 'votes own clue' assumption the stage states. Own node with the Demo guilt(): g = 0 gives 0.0730 = 7%, g = 1 gives 0.3000 = 30%, g = 2 gives 0.7000 = 70%. The bar label 'Chance of guilt from all three clues' now matches on all three states. The pass 21 bug is fixed.

claims.text: Because the other jurors vote their clues, being pivotal tells you that both of their clues said guilty, evidence a juror who just votes their own clue throws away.
claims.source: Under sincere voting a guilty vote occurs exactly when the clue says guilty; pivotal = both others guilty = both clues guilty. E&K ch. 23 (pivotal-voter reasoning); Feddersen and Pesendorfer (1998), Am. Political Science Rev. 92(1), from the brief, not opened by builder. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Re-derived: under sincere voting a guilty vote occurs iff the clue says guilty, so pivotal implies both clues guilty. E&K (2010) ch. 23 (Voting; jury decisions and unanimity) placement from memory, confident; Feddersen & Pesendorfer (1998), APSR 92(1), from memory, not opened; the sentence rests on the derivation.

claims.text: Your vote moves the verdict, never the bar: it is not a clue. (Stage: 'Votes are not clues.')
claims.source: Builder (2026-10-14, v3): in Demo.tsx the bar is guilt(g, 3 - g) where g counts only the other jurors' guilty clues (they vote their clues); your clue is fixed innocent and `mine` (your vote) enters only verdictGuilty. In the model your vote carries no information about guilt. Unverified. | FC pass 24 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Read Demo.tsx: the bar is guilt(g, 3 - g) with g counted from the other two jurors only; 'mine' enters only verdictGuilty, so 'Flip your vote' changes Verdict (when pivotal) and never the bar. In the model your vote carries no information, so 'it is not a clue' holds. Note for the builder (not a dispute): the stage line's general form 'Votes are not clues.' sits awkwardly with the reveal's point that the others' votes reveal their clues; 'Your vote is not a clue.' would say exactly what c5 claims.

recall.question: Under a unanimity rule, when does your single vote change a jury's verdict, and what does that tell you?
options: Always; it tells you nothing about the others
Only when every other juror votes to convict, which is evidence of guilt
Only when the jury is split evenly
recall.why: One acquittal is enough to acquit, so your vote decides only when all others convict, and their convicting votes carry their guilty clues.
